Kirsten Neuschafer our Golden Girl

By: Liz Fish | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Sitting around a campfire on a wild beach we spend time getting into the head of Kirsten Neuschafer - the first women- 1st South African to win the most challenging solo yacht race in the world- the G

Unique Selling Point:
Kirsten Neuschafer wins the Golden Globe Race - making South Africa proud! She is the first woman to win this solo around the globe race –the most challenging competition the sailing world has to offer. It took 235 days in her 36ft yacht Minnehaha, crossing the finishing line in Les Sables d’Olonne on Freedom Day. What makes this a unique race is that it’s done the old fashion way, the way Joshua Slocum did it in 1898 - no GPS, no modern navigational tools, totally unassisted, without weather reports, or knowing where her competitors are. She had to use old-school sextants and star charts and the only satellite calls allowed were with race officials. Right until she crossed the line, she had no idea she had been in the lead for several weeks.

Summary:
Apart from navigating extreme weather she also stopped to rescue fellow competitor, veteran Finnish sailor Tapio Lehtinen, after his yacht sank in the southern Indian Ocean. She managed to find him adrift in his dinghy in huge seas and then got him safely to the closest ship - a feat all in itself.
Sixteen yachts set sail in the race, only three arrived at the finish. The end was a scary, foggy night in the busy shipping lanes - it was not over until she sailed in, with her mother waiting on the dock to meet her.
At home in Gqeberha to see her father, her dog and her friends we catch up with her around her campfire as she sets off on her walk along the Wild Coast, free camping under the stars. Kirsten has the most indominable spirit, believing in her inner voice. Before taking on the world’s toughest yacht race, she cycled solo across Africa at the age of 22. She wanted to get home from Europe and didnt have much money so she bought a bicycle and set off.. Everyone warned her that she would die of thirst in the Sahara, or be raped and killed. But she arrived safely in Cape Agulus and pretty soon decided her next landscape was the sea.
Her words of wisdom on the podium were that 80% of the race is in the preparation before the race - she spent months fixing up her boat and knew every inch of it before she set sail. And once on the water, she said, it’s constant maintenance, including scrapping barnacles off the hull in freezing water.
Asked how she felt about being the first woman to win the race, she replied “well, I am a skipper - and yes I guess I am a woman.” She is winning a special trophy as the 1st women to win the race - which she thinks is a bit odd- a bit like a "disability" prize.

Crossing the finish line of the Golden Globe Race on the boat sailing in – all the fanfare and celebration including hugging her mother on the dock
Script: Kirsten Neuschafer making history!
The first South African and woman to win the most extreme yacht race in the world- the Golden Globe
235 days at sea, nonstop - solo - and unassisted. Facing fear - incredible deprivation - completely alone.
16 set sail - only 3 crossed the finish line in France
Kirsten : It's a moment that I'll never forget…, you know, after eight months all alone and just, you know, I'd achieved my goal. I'd done what I wanted to do. So that was really, really amazing.
Annette: it was spectacular and just feeling her cheek on my cheek was unbelievable.
Upsound and establisher back on the beach
Script: Back home in Gqeberha - escaping the media hype- Kirsten is setting off on another lone quest - hiking along the wild coast with her beloved dog Dwesa. We joined her coffee and a chat on the beach.
Erin “Hi Kirsten
Kirsten Hi Erin
Erin “World winning golden globe world champion now sitting on the beach making a fire”
Kirsten “ From champion to skollie on the beach” laugher
Erin: Are you looking forward to that peace and quiet after what's been a bit of a whirlwind I imagine?
Kirsten: Yeah, I sure am. I'm going to not take my cell phone with me, and I'm going to enjoy feeling land under my feet and watching the swell. The breaking waves, which you prefer, not watching when you're at sea.
Script: Back to their stomping ground, the Wild Coast is one of her favorite places in the world. Alone - no commitments, no cameras, no deadlines.
Time to breathe out - after an intense three years.
Kirsten “It's been eating, sleeping, dreaming of just this whole project and even if it meant working until 2 or 3 in the morning. Yeah, whatever it took.
Script: And it takes everything.
In 1968 - when the world's attention was on the first moon landing, nine men set sail on the first solo non-stop sailing race around the World.
Only one finished - 29 year old Robin Knox Johnston. This is only the 3rd race since 1968, strictly using the same technology, and boats that are more than 35 years old. Even the prize money remains as it was - a princely - 5000 pounds

Kirsten that’s the beauty of this race, it’s not about how fast you can be or high tech your boat its about, are you going to find your way around the world, are you going to avoid dangers you know it's also a survival race.
Script: For the last 40 years people have depended on navigating with a GPS, and detailed advanced weather warnings.
Link: This is sailing stripped to the bare essentials- think old school. No GPS, navigating by the sun, a wrist watch and a sextant . And music - strictly cassette tapes.
Kirsten ” 08.16 Getting the weather forecast from Cape Town radio it’s the best weather forecast that I have been able to get information up until now
upsound
Script: Often with no idea of what kind of weather was coming at her, or where her fellow contestants were, until she crossed the finish line - Kirsten - never let up.
Kirsten I've got no racing background. So it was in the back of my mind the whole time. Keep going faster, keep going faster, Keep a balance between enjoying the ride, keeping the boat safe, staying well rested, but pushing it as hard as I could
Preparing for a storm isn’t a 10 minute job and perhaps in the dark and in the rain its not going to be a lot of fun
Kirsten And I like the fact of having to think about how am I going to do this all on my own with just two hands? How am I going to be on the bow and on the stern of the boat simultaneously?
Upsound
Kirsten … you would have seen me talking to myself quite a bit. Like I'd give myself instructions as I would a crew I'd say, for example, … it's really time you got the spinnaker up now get up now and do it. It has to be done now. And then I'd say, okay, I'm going already
I'd speak to the wind like, please, wind, please come back. Don't leave me here. You know I need you that kind of thing
Script: Kirsten’s been pushing the limits from early childhood - her mother Annette, just leant to hold on - for the ride.
Annette: Kirsten actually taught me to be a lot less fearful. And she's really tried to toughen me up. From a very early age, she was just crazy about the sea and just felt at one with it, really….. She actually bought a hobby cat with a friend, and they had this idea that they were going to kind of see how far they could get up the West Coast and in Yzerfontein they wrecked their whole boat because it was just not stable enough for those seas
Kirsten- it's funny how one craves things from home from time to time good thing I took a supply of mielie pap from South Africa when I left
Script: Her father Zigi took her sailing from a very young age - but now in his mid 80’s he is battling a neurological condition.
Kirsten My father, it had actually been his dream to sail around the world.
Erin: Did you think about him and that dream he had as a young man during your travels
Kirsten: Yeah, I did. You know, I thought about, for example, how much he would have liked to have had the opportunity to sail around Cape Horn because that's like a the ultimate thing for a sailor to do and at least he would be happy to know that I am doing it
Kirsten “So there is Cape Horn – there- there we have it- pretty exciting moment
Link: Kirsten is hard core at 22 she cycled home from Europe across Africa her first big adventure. That 15 000 km solo trip inspired her to follow her heart
Kirsten People told me that it's crazy that you're not going to make it. And it's like, Well, let me at least try. And I think that's the starting point is just at least try.
Annette: I just suddenly realized how determined she was to do this race and how hardworking she is and how disciplined she has remained.
Script: Despite briefly sailing in-shore in Cape Town, race rules said no-one was allowed on or off the yacht. But she did see friends and family.
Kirsten Now that I am on the way again after having just waved at them briefly I feel lonelier than I have on the whole trip
Erin: What is it about who you are that allows you to really manage those moments?
Kirsten: for me when I'm in a city and no one's making eye contact with me and no one's talking to me, that's when I feel lonely so the majority of the time on this trip I felt solitude but I felt it in a way that's I could commune more with nature rather than I was craving other human company.
Script: Ironically - a distress call put Kirsten in contact with another human, in the most dramatic - and unexpected way
LINK Getting that distress call galvanised Kirsten into action. Her fellow contestant Tapio Lehtinen yacht had sunk. He was bobbing around in a life raft in the Southern ocean
Kirsten We are on our way to see if we can find Tapio
Kirsten: Well for one I was really happy when I finally spotted him because the liferaft had a VHF in it so he kept on saying, I can see you, I can see you. And I'm like, I can't see you for the life of me, I can't see you
Script: She undertook the extremely scary task of offloading him onto a passing ship.
Kirsten Then I cut the lines on my side . I had to get away from that ship really, really quickly. I didn't want to be stuck. Between Tapio’s raft with my boat and then the big ship.
So yey so now he is on the ship on his way to China
Script: And then - what sailors have feared most - for centuries.
Link: You know that expression down in the doldrums- this is literally where it comes from. Stuck in the middle of a race for 2 weeks going nowhere
Kirsten Yip thats it dead calm
Kirsten 00:32:21:29 - So if I was really getting frustrated to the point that I wanted to rip my hair out... I just jump over the side and swim until I was out of breath,…. and then look back at the boat and say, Ah, that looks a bit small I had better get back to the boat get back to the boat climb up and then you have got a bit of adrenaline anyway because it gets a bit creepy after awhile…
Script: Eventually - the wind returned
Kirsten There is such sincerity behind a lot of the messages that people have sent me where I almost feel guilty because they're saying such lovely things to me….ultimately I went out there and did what I wanted to. It was about me, myself and I but I am sure it had a really positive impact on me being all on my own out there to having people behind the scenes say yeeh we rooting for you we hope you win.
Although it was a solo race, .. there were a lot of people behind me to make it happen for me. So somewhere I'd like to give back.

Promo 11 She won the world’s toughest yacht race breaking so many records- 1st South Africa, 1st women and her 1st race. Kirsten Neuschafer achieved her dream
Promo 21 sec “ Facing hardship, deprivation and isolation - what does it take to sail around the globe solo in extreme weather?
Preparing for a storm isn’t a 10 minute job and perhaps in the dark and in the rain its not going to be a lot of fun
Script: Without a GPS or advanced weather warnings

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Sitting around a campfire on a wild beach we spend time getting into the head of Kirsten Neuschafer - the first women- 1st South African to win the most challenging solo yacht race in the world- the G
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Kirsten Neuschafer wins the Golden Globe Race - making South Africa proud! She is the first woman to win this solo around the globe race –the most challenging competition the sailing world has to offer. It took 235 days in her 36ft yacht Minnehaha, crossing the finishing line in Les Sables d’Olonne on Freedom Day. What makes this a unique race is that it’s done the old fashion way, the way Joshua Slocum did it in 1898 - no GPS, no modern navigational tools, totally unassisted, without weather reports, or knowing where her competitors are. She had to use old-school sextants and star charts and the only satellite calls allowed were with race officials. Right until she crossed the line, she had no idea she had been in the lead for several weeks.
metadata.Summary: Apart from navigating extreme weather she also stopped to rescue fellow competitor, veteran Finnish sailor Tapio Lehtinen, after his yacht sank in the southern Indian Ocean. She managed to find him adrift in his dinghy in huge seas and then got him safely to the closest ship - a feat all in itself. Sixteen yachts set sail in the race, only three arrived at the finish. The end was a scary, foggy night in the busy shipping lanes - it was not over until she sailed in, with her mother waiting on the dock to meet her. At home in Gqeberha to see her father, her dog and her friends we catch up with her around her campfire as she sets off on her walk along the Wild Coast, free camping under the stars. Kirsten has the most indominable spirit, believing in her inner voice. Before taking on the world’s toughest yacht race, she cycled solo across Africa at the age of 22. She wanted to get home from Europe and didnt have much money so she bought a bicycle and set off.. Everyone warned her that she would die of thirst in the Sahara, or be raped and killed. But she arrived safely in Cape Agulus and pretty soon decided her next landscape was the sea. Her words of wisdom on the podium were that 80% of the race is in the preparation before the race - she spent months fixing up her boat and knew every inch of it before she set sail. And once on the water, she said, it’s constant maintenance, including scrapping barnacles off the hull in freezing water. Asked how she felt about being the first woman to win the race, she replied “well, I am a skipper - and yes I guess I am a woman.” She is winning a special trophy as the 1st women to win the race - which she thinks is a bit odd- a bit like a "disability" prize.
